analogy.p: Imagine a tall pile of books: the book at the bottom has to support the weight of every book above it, while the book at the top supports almost nothing. In the same way, a layer of water deep down supports the weight of all the water above it, so the pressure is higher. The atmosphere is like a pile of foam mattresses: the bottom ones are squashed (dense), the top ones are fluffy (thin), so the bottom layers take the greatest load. The analogy breaks down because pressure in a fluid acts in all directions, not only downwards, and a pile of books does not push sideways.
analogy.t: A pile of people (or a stack of books)

bullets: **Fluid** = liquid or gas (both can flow and take the shape of their container).
**Pressure** = force acting normally (at right angles) on a surface divided by the area of that surface.
The SI unit of pressure is the **pascal (Pa)**; 1 Pa = 1 N/m2 (one newton on every square metre).
Pressure is a **scalar**: it has size but no direction, even though the force it produces does have a direction.
Larger forces and smaller areas both increase pressure; this is why a knife edge cuts and snow shoes stop you sinking.
Solids transmit force in one direction, but fluids push outwards on all the walls of the container at once.
Common units: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa; atmospheric pressure at sea level is roughly 101 000 Pa (101 kPa).
core.h: What is a fluid, and what is pressure?
core.p: A **fluid** is any substance that can flow: it can be either a **liquid** or a **gas**. Because the particles in a fluid can move past each other, a fluid takes the shape of its container and pushes on every surface it touches. The specification asks you to know that the pressure in a fluid causes a **force normal (at right angles) to any surface**. Pressure tells you how concentrated a force is: the same force spread over a bigger area gives a smaller pressure. This is a Physics-only topic, so it appears in AQA Paper 2 for those sitting the triple award.

bullets: p = F / A where p is pressure (Pa), F is force normal to the surface (N), A is area (m2).
Rearrangements: F = p x A and A = F / p; use a triangle with F on top and p and A below if helpful.
Unit conversion: 1 m2 = 10 000 cm2, so 20 cm2 = 0.0020 m2. Doing this wrongly loses a mark every time.
Example: 600 N spread over 0.30 m2 gives p = 600 / 0.30 = 2000 Pa.
Halving the area doubles the pressure for the same force; doubling the force doubles the pressure for the same area.
In a fluid the force from the pressure on any surface = pressure x area of that surface, which is how we find the force on a dam, window or hatch.
Always state the unit; Pa and N/m2 are equivalent and both are accepted.
core.p: The core relationship you must be able to recall and use is **pressure = force normal to a surface / area of that surface**, written p = F / A. Pressure is in pascals (Pa), force in newtons (N) and area in square metres (m2). Examiners often give areas in cm2 or mm2, so converting to m2 is a frequent hidden step. The equation can be rearranged to F = p A and A = F / p, and it works for solids as well as fluids, which is why it links to this topic.

bullets: Pressure comes from the **collisions of fluid particles** with a surface; many collisions per second give a steady force.
Each collision pushes at right angles to the surface (the particle rebounds along the normal).
The more frequent or more energetic the collisions, the greater the pressure.
At a given point inside a fluid the pressure is the same in every direction.
This is why a punctured container squirts water out sideways as well as downwards.
Pressure force is shown on diagrams as arrows perpendicular to the wall; arrow length can be used to show the size of the pressure.
Do not say pressure only acts downwards; this is a common error.
core.h: Why fluid pressure acts at right angles to surfaces
core.p: Fluid particles are in constant random motion and collide with the walls of their container. Each collision exerts a tiny force on the wall, and at the instant of collision that force is perpendicular to the surface because the particle bounces back off it. There are enormous numbers of particles and collisions every second, so the total effect averages out to a steady force on the wall. This is why the pressure force always acts at **right angles (normal)** to any surface, whether it is the side, base or lid of a container. Explaining pressure in terms of particle collisions is a key mark-scheme idea.

bullets: **Pressure in a liquid increases with depth** because the weight of liquid above the point increases.
The pressure at a point is caused by the weight of the column of liquid above it, acting in all directions.
At the surface of the liquid (from the liquid alone) the pressure is zero; it grows steadily as you go down.
In a bottle with holes at different heights, the lowest jet shoots out furthest because the pressure is highest there.
The increase is linear with depth for a liquid of constant density: doubling the depth doubles the pressure from the liquid.
Gases behave differently because their density changes with height (see atmospheric pressure).
Mark-scheme phrasing: "the deeper the water, the greater the weight (or mass) of water above, so the greater the pressure".
core.h: Why pressure increases with depth in a liquid
core.p: In a liquid, the pressure at a point depends on how much liquid lies above it. The deeper you go, the greater the **weight of the column of liquid** pressing down on that level, and that weight is transmitted through the fluid in all directions. Equivalently, there are more particles above a deeper point, and the lower layers must support those above them, so they are squeezed together more strongly and collide with greater force. This is why a diver feels more pressure on their ears at 10 m than at 1 m, and why water squirts out faster from a hole low down a container.

bullets: p = h ρ g where p is pressure (Pa), h is height or depth of column (m), ρ is density (kg/m3), g is gravitational field strength (N/kg).
On Earth g = 9.8 N/kg (use the value given in the question; 9.8 is standard in AQA papers).
Density of fresh water is 1000 kg/m3; seawater is about 1030 kg/m3, so pressure in the sea rises slightly faster with depth.
Doubling the depth doubles the pressure; doubling the density doubles the pressure.
A denser liquid (e.g. mercury, about 13 600 kg/m3) gives much more pressure at the same depth than water.
On the Moon g is smaller, so the pressure at the same depth in the same liquid would be less.
Depth means the vertical distance below the surface, not the length of a sloping container.
core.h: Factors affecting pressure in a liquid: depth, density and g
core.p: The pressure due to a column of liquid depends on three things: the **height (depth) of the column**, the **density of the liquid** and the **gravitational field strength**. It does not depend on the shape of the container or on the total amount of liquid. The relationship is **pressure due to a column of liquid = height of column x density of liquid x gravitational field strength**, p = h ρ g. This is a Physics-only equation, so make sure you can use it confidently.

bullets: Step 1: volume of column V = A x h.
Step 2: mass m = density x volume = ρ A h.
Step 3: weight W = m g = ρ A h g (this is the downward force on area A).
Step 4: p = F / A = ρ A h g / A = h ρ g.
Because A cancels, a wide lake and a narrow tube of the same depth have the same pressure at the bottom.
This explains why the very wide base of a dam holds the same pressure per metre of depth as a narrow pipe.
Check units: m x kg/m3 x N/kg = N/m2 = Pa, which confirms the equation is dimensionally correct.
core.h: Deriving p = h ρ g (Higher tier reasoning)
core.p: The equation can be derived from p = F / A. Consider a column of liquid with base area A and height h. Its volume is A h, so its mass is m = ρ V = ρ A h, and its weight is W = m g = ρ A h g. This weight is the force on the base area A, so p = W / A = ρ A h g / A = **h ρ g**. The base area cancels, which proves that pressure depends only on depth, density and g, not on the width or shape of the container. Being able to explain this derivation earns the reasoning marks in Higher-tier questions.

bullets: Difference in pressure Δp = (h2 - h1) ρ g, where h2 and h1 are the two depths.
Example: a diver goes from 4 m to 24 m in seawater (ρ = 1030): Δh = 20 m, Δp = 20 x 1030 x 9.8 = 201 880 Pa (about 2.0 x 10^5 Pa).
Each extra 10 m of water adds about 98 000 Pa (roughly one more atmosphere).
The difference does not depend on the starting depth, only on how far you move vertically.
Convert units first: depths in cm must be changed to m.
Give the answer to a sensible number of significant figures (usually matching the data, often 2 or 3 s.f.).
If the question asks for the total pressure, add atmospheric pressure to the pressure from the liquid.
core.h: Calculating differences in pressure at different depths (Higher tier)
core.p: The specification (Higher tier) asks you to calculate the **differences in pressure at different depths** in a liquid. You simply apply p = h ρ g to the difference in depth: Δp = Δh x ρ x g. This is very useful, for example for a diver descending, a submarine changing depth or a hole at one level compared with another. Take care to subtract the depths, not add, and to keep the same liquid density throughout the calculation.

bullets: Same depth in the same liquid means same pressure, regardless of container shape or width.
The total weight of liquid in a wide container is bigger, but the base area is bigger too, so the pressure is the same.
Total force on a base differs: force = pressure x area, so the wide base experiences a larger force.
Pressure acts equally in all directions at a given depth (sideways, upwards and downwards).
A sloping container does not change the pressure: use the vertical depth, not the slant length.
Water in connected tubes reaches the same level because equal depths give equal pressures.
Common exam mistake: saying a bigger volume of water gives a bigger pressure; it does not.
core.h: Pressure and shape: the same at the same depth
core.p: In a liquid at rest, the pressure depends on depth only. All points at the same depth in the same liquid have the same pressure, whatever the shape of the container, and whether the point is near a wall or the middle. This follows from p = h ρ g because shape does not appear in the equation. It explains why water finds its own level in connected containers, and why a tall thin tube of water can create the same base pressure as a wide pool.

bullets: Liquids: particles close together, difficult to compress, nearly constant density.
Gases: particles far apart, easy to compress, density changes with pressure and height.
Pressure in a liquid increases uniformly with depth; in the atmosphere it decreases non-uniformly (faster at first) with height.
The density of air at sea level is about 1.2 kg/m3, over 800 times less than water, so air pressure changes slowly over small heights.
Both fluids exert pressure through particle collisions with surfaces.
Gas pressure inside a container is due to particle collisions on the walls (linked to the gas pressure topic in particle model).
This is why p = h ρ g is only used for liquids at GCSE.
core.p: Liquids and gases are both fluids, but they differ in how their density behaves. A liquid is almost **incompressible**, so its density is virtually constant and pressure rises in a simple straight-line way with depth. A gas is easily compressed, so its density is not constant: air near the ground is squashed by the air above, and gets thinner as you rise. That is why the equation p = h ρ g works neatly for liquids but cannot be used simply for the whole atmosphere.

bullets: Atmospheric pressure is caused by **air molecules colliding with a surface**.
Air molecules are held near the Earth by gravity, so the atmosphere has weight.
Sea level pressure is roughly 101 kPa (about 1 atmosphere); the force is about 10 N per cm2.
We do not feel it because the pressure inside our bodies is balanced with the outside.
Atmospheric pressure acts in all directions, not just downwards.
It changes slightly with the weather (high and low pressure systems) as well as with altitude.
Everyday evidence: a drinking straw works because lowering pressure in the straw lets atmospheric pressure push the drink up.
core.p: The Earth is surrounded by a layer of air called the **atmosphere**. Air is a mixture of gas particles (mostly nitrogen and oxygen) that are constantly moving and colliding with every surface, including your body. These collisions create **atmospheric pressure**, which acts at right angles to surfaces. You can also think of it as the weight of the column of air above the surface. At sea level it is about 101 000 Pa, which is equal to a force of about 10 N on every square centimetre of surface.

bullets: Higher up, there are fewer air molecules above, so the weight of air above is less.
The air is less dense at altitude, so fewer molecules hit a surface each second, giving a lower pressure.
Pressure falls quickly at first: about half of the air by weight lies within roughly the lowest 5.5 km.
At the top of Mount Everest (8.8 km) the pressure is about a third of sea level, which is why climbers need oxygen.
In space (vacuum) there are almost no particles, so almost no pressure.
The fall in gravity with height is tiny and is NOT the reason for the pressure drop.
Link: the graph of pressure against height is a downward curve, not a straight line, because air is compressible.
core.h: Why atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude
core.p: The specification asks you to explain why atmospheric pressure **decreases with increasing height**. There are two linked reasons. First, as you go higher there is less air above you, so the weight of the column of air above is smaller. Second, the atmosphere gets thinner: the **density of the air decreases** with height, so there are fewer air molecules per cubic metre and fewer collisions per second with a surface. The atmosphere does not stop at a sharp edge; it fades gradually into space where the pressure is effectively zero.

bullets: Total pressure at depth = atmospheric pressure + pressure due to the liquid column (p = h ρ g).
Dams are wider at the bottom because pressure, and so force on the wall, is greatest there.
Divers feel pressure on their eardrums; equalising removes the difference between inside and outside.
Deep-sea submersibles need strong, rounded hulls because of enormous pressures (about 1 atmosphere extra per 10 m).
Aircraft cabins are pressurised because outside pressure at cruising height is far below sea-level pressure.
Water towers are placed high so that taps at the bottom have a high water pressure from the height of the column.
Suction cups and drinking straws work because atmospheric pressure pushes, not because "suction pulls".
core.p: In real life the pressure on a diver is the pressure from the water plus atmospheric pressure pressing on the water surface. So the total pressure at 10 m below the surface of a lake is roughly 101 000 + 98 000 = 199 000 Pa, almost double the surface value. These ideas explain why dams are thicker at the base, why submarines need strong hulls, why your ears hurt in deep water or on a plane, and why aircraft cabins are pressurised.

bullets: Density: ρ = m / V (particle model) is needed for p = h ρ g.
Weight: W = m g links to the derivation of pressure in a liquid column.
Upthrust: the pressure at the bottom of a submerged object is greater than at the top, giving a resultant upward force.
Gas pressure (Physics only): pressure changes with volume at constant temperature (p V = constant).
Kinetic theory: temperature and particle speeds change gas pressure in sealed containers.
Forces: pressure is force per unit area, and the force is found by F = p A.
Energy and work: pumping fluids against pressure requires work to be done.
core.p: Fluid pressure connects with several other parts of the course. It uses p = F / A and weight = mass x gravitational field strength from forces, density from particle model of matter, and the particle collision explanation of gas pressure. It also underpins upthrust, floating and sinking, because upthrust arises from a pressure difference between the top and the bottom of a submerged object. Understanding these links lets you tackle multi-step questions.

exam: Command words: "State/Give" = 1 mark recall; "Explain" = a reason using because/so; "Calculate" = show equation, substitution and answer with unit.
Learn the Physics-only equation p = h ρ g and write it out first in any calculation: mark 1 for the equation, 1 for substitution, 1 for the answer and unit.
For "explain why pressure increases with depth" (2 marks): deeper means more liquid (greater weight) above (1); so more force on each unit area (1).
For "explain why atmospheric pressure decreases with height" (3 marks): fewer air molecules above / thinner atmosphere (1); lower density (1); fewer collisions with a surface per second (1).
A 4-mark explanation should link: collisions of particles, force normal to the surface, and pressure = force per area, and use the words "weight of the column".
In a 6-mark question, structure your answer: definition, cause (particles / weight), equation, effect of changing each factor, real-life example.
Data/graph tips: a pressure-depth graph for a liquid is a straight line through the origin; the gradient is ρ g (so you can find density).
A pressure-height graph for the atmosphere is a curve that falls and levels off towards zero; do not draw a straight line.
Always give the unit (Pa or kPa); if the answer is a large number, give it in standard form (e.g. 2.0 x 10^5 Pa).
Use g = 9.8 N/kg unless the question gives another value; if data are 2 s.f., give a 2 s.f. answer.
Check estimates: 10 m of water is about 1 atmosphere (about 100 kPa extra), a good sanity check.

mistakes.r: It depends only on the depth, the density of the liquid and g; shape and total volume do not matter.
mistakes.w: Pressure in a liquid depends on how much water there is (the volume or total mass).

mistakes.r: Pressure acts in all directions, at right angles to any surface it touches.
There are fewer air molecules above and the air is less dense, so fewer collisions per second with a surface.
mistakes.w: Atmospheric pressure drops with height because gravity gets weaker.

mistakes.r: Pressure is lower, not zero; it only approaches zero in space where there is almost no air.
mistakes.w: There is no atmospheric pressure at the top of a mountain.

mistakes.r: Convert to metres and square metres (1 m2 = 10 000 cm2) so the answer is in Pa.
mistakes.w: Using depth in cm or area in cm2 directly in the equations.

mistakes.r: It decreases, and not in a straight line: air density falls with height so the curve gets shallower.
mistakes.w: Pressure increases linearly with height in the atmosphere.

mistakes.r: At the same depth in the same liquid, the pressure is the same; only the total force on the base is larger.
mistakes.w: A wider container has a higher pressure at the bottom.

mistakes.r: Total pressure = atmospheric pressure + pressure from the liquid (h ρ g).
mistakes.w: Forgetting to add atmospheric pressure when asked for total pressure.

summary: The specification asks you to explain that a fluid (liquid or gas) exerts pressure at right angles to any surface, why pressure in a liquid increases with depth and how it depends on density, to use p = h ρ g and calculate pressure differences (Higher tier), and to explain why atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude. It matters because these ideas explain dams, divers, submarines, mountains and aircraft, and are a regular source of calculation and explanation marks in Paper 2.

terms.d: A substance that can flow: a liquid or a gas.
Force acting normally (at right angles) on a surface per unit area: p = F / A.
The SI unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N/m2.
At right angles (perpendicular) to a surface.
Mass per unit volume of a substance: ρ = m / V, measured in kg/m3.
Force per unit mass in a gravitational field; 9.8 N/kg at the Earth's surface.
The vertical distance below the surface of a fluid.
The imaginary vertical stack of liquid above a point, whose weight causes the pressure there.
Cannot easily be squashed into a smaller volume; liquids are almost incompressible.
The layer of gases surrounding the Earth, held in place by gravity.
The pressure caused by air molecules colliding with a surface; also described as the weight of the column of air above.
A region with no (or almost no) particles, so almost no pressure.
The force of gravity on an object: W = m g.
The difference between the pressures at two points, e.g. Δp = Δh ρ g in a liquid.

worked.q: A swimming pool is 2.5 m deep and filled with fresh water (density 1000 kg/m3, g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the pressure due to the water at the bottom of the pool. (b) A drain cover at the bottom has area 0.040 m2. Calculate the force on it. [5 marks]
steps: Equation: p = h ρ g (1 mark).
Force: F = p A = 24 500 x 0.040 (1 mark).

worked.q: A diver descends from a depth of 4.0 m to 24 m in the sea (density 1030 kg/m3, g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate the increase in pressure. [4 marks, Higher tier]
steps: Change in depth Δh = 24 - 4.0 = 20 m (1 mark).
Use Δp = Δh ρ g (1 mark).
Δp = 201 880 Pa, about 2.0 x 10^5 Pa (1 mark).

worked.ans: Model answer: Atmospheric pressure is caused by air molecules colliding with a surface. At the top of a mountain the atmosphere above is thinner, so there is less air above and the air has a lower density. There are therefore fewer molecules hitting the surface each second, so the force per unit area, the pressure, is lower.
worked.q: Explain why atmospheric pressure is lower at the top of a mountain than at sea level. [4 marks]
steps: Marker idea 1: air is a gas made of particles that collide with surfaces, producing a force at right angles to them.
Marker idea 2: higher up, there is less air above, so the weight of the column of air is smaller.
Marker idea 3: the air is less dense (thinner) at altitude, so fewer molecules per cubic metre.
Marker idea 4: fewer collisions per second with a surface, so a smaller force per unit area (lower pressure).
